package_info.package_manager: Custom/Unknown (malware targeting ICS/SCADA devices, not distributed via public package managers)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (modular malware suite, not versioned in the traditional sense)
package_info.why_malicious: The malware suite is specifically engineered to compromise, disrupt, and manipulate industrial control systems (ICS) and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) devices. It enables attackers to enumerate, control, and sabotage critical infrastructure by exploiting device protocols, brute-forcing credentials, and leveraging known vulnerabilities in engineering workstations. The suite's modular tools provide full system access, lateral movement, and device manipulation capabilities, representing a severe and targeted threat to operational technology environments.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when executed on an engineering workstation or within an ICS network

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode representing TAGRUN OPC UA scanner behavior
connect_to_opc_ua_server(target_ip)
enumerate_tags_and_structure()
brute_force_credentials()
read_tag_values()
write_tag_values()
malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudocode (actual implementation likely C/C++ or Python)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code connects to OPC UA servers, enumerates their structure and tags, brute-forces credentials, and reads/writes tag values, enabling unauthorized access and manipulation of industrial process data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs bulk enumeration of OPC UA tags, brute-forces authentication, and executes unauthorized read/write operations on process data, which are clear indicators of reconnaissance and manipulation activity not associated with legitimate engineering tasks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate engineering tools do not brute-force credentials or indiscriminately enumerate and manipulate all tags on a production system without proper authentication and authorization.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Engineering tools may enumerate tags and read/write values during commissioning or troubleshooting, but only with authenticated access and under controlled circumstances, never via brute-force or unscheduled access.
key_indicators: Brute-force authentication attempts against OPC UA servers
Bulk enumeration of OPC UA tags and structure
Unauthorized read/write operations on process tags

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode representing CODECALL Modbus attack behavior
connect_to_modicon_plc(target_ip)
scan_device()
read_plc_memory()
write_plc_memory()
issue_control_commands()
malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudocode (actual implementation likely C/C++ or Python)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code connects to Schneider Electric Modicon PLCs using the Modbus protocol, scans devices, reads and writes PLC memory, and issues control commands, resulting in unauthorized device manipulation and potential process sabotage.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly reading and writing PLC memory and issuing control commands outside of authorized engineering sessions is highly suspicious and can disrupt or damage industrial processes, indicating malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal engineering software does not perform unscheduled or unauthorized memory manipulation or control command execution on PLCs, especially without proper authentication and change management.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use may occur during device commissioning or maintenance, but only by authorized personnel with proper authentication and within scheduled windows.
key_indicators: Unauthorized Modbus protocol connections to PLCs
Direct PLC memory manipulation outside of maintenance windows
Unscheduled control command execution on PLCs

malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudocode (actual implementation likely C/C++ or Python)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code connects to Omron PLCs and servo drives, scans devices, reads and writes servo drive parameters, enabling unauthorized manipulation of industrial machinery operation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unauthorized access and manipulation of servo drive parameters can cause physical damage or unsafe operation of industrial equipment, representing a direct threat to safety and process integrity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal operations do not involve unscheduled or unauthorized parameter changes on servo drives; such actions are strictly controlled and logged.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate engineering tasks may involve parameter changes, but only under strict controls, with proper authentication, and during scheduled maintenance.
key_indicators: Unauthorized Omron PLC or servo drive access
Unscheduled parameter manipulation on servo drives

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when executed on a Windows engineering workstation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode representing ASRock driver exploit
load_vulnerable_asrock_driver()
exploit_driver_to_escalate_privileges()
gain_system_access()
malicious_snippets.code_language: pseudocode (actual implementation likely C/C++ or PowerShell)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code loads a vulnerable ASRock motherboard driver and exploits it to escalate privileges on the Windows engineering workstation, resulting in full system compromise and enabling deployment of further attack modules.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exploiting known vulnerable drivers for privilege escalation is a well-documented malware technique and is never part of normal engineering workstation operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not load or exploit vulnerable drivers to gain elevated privileges; such actions are strictly prohibited and monitored.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; privilege escalation via driver exploit is always malicious and has no legitimate use case.
key_indicators: Loading of known vulnerable ASRock driver
Privilege escalation attempts via driver exploitation

attack_chain.action: Initial compromise of engineering workstation, possibly via phishing or supply chain attack.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malware components on the workstation

attack_chain.action: Privilege escalation on engineering workstation using ASRock driver exploit.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full system access and ability to deploy ICS attack modules

attack_chain.action: Network reconnaissance and enumeration of ICS/SCADA devices (OPC UA servers, PLCs).
Brute-force credentials and gain unauthorized access to ICS devices.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to read/write tag values and manipulate device state

attack_chain.action: Manipulation of PLC memory, tag values, and servo drive parameters to disrupt or sabotage industrial processes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Disruption, degradation, or damage to ICS/SCADA operations (final goal)

behavioral_signatures: Bulk enumeration of OPC UA tags and structure from engineering workstations
Brute-force authentication attempts against OPC UA servers originating from non-standard sources
Unauthorized Modbus protocol activity targeting PLCs outside of scheduled maintenance windows
Unscheduled or unauthorized read/write operations on PLC memory or servo drive parameters
Loading and exploitation of known vulnerable ASRock motherboard drivers for privilege escalation
file_indicators: Presence of unknown or unsigned binaries on engineering workstations
Unexpected driver files related to ASRock hardware in system directories
Malware components named TAGRUN, CODECALL, OMSHELL, EVILSCHOLAR, BADOMEN, DUSTTUNNEL, MOUSEHOLE, LAZYCARGO
network_indicators: Unusual OPC UA and Modbus network traffic originating from engineering workstations
Connections to PLCs and OPC UA servers outside of scheduled maintenance or authorized engineering sessions
Lateral movement within OT networks from compromised workstations
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor engineering workstations and OT networks for unauthorized enumeration of OPC UA tags, brute-force authentication attempts, and unscheduled Modbus/Omron protocol activity. Detect loading of vulnerable ASRock drivers and privilege escalation attempts. Flag any binaries or processes matching known malware component names or exhibiting these behaviors. Correlate network activity with scheduled maintenance to identify suspicious access patterns. Implement endpoint and network monitoring to alert on these specific behavioral, file, and network indicators.
